finding.claim: The app takes the caller's identity from a client-supplied HTTP header and does not authenticate it. Any client can send X-Session-User-Verified with another user's name and pass the ACL checks as that user. This is exploitable unless a trusted front proxy strips and sets the header. Nothing in this code enforces that.
finding.source: The attacker-controlled request header X-Session-User-Verified. The precondition is direct network access to the app, or a proxy that forwards the client's own copy of the header.
finding.sink: The delete at views.py:18 (del STORE[fid]) and the rename at views.py:27 (f["name"] = ...), both gated by the ACL on g.user.

trace.note: before_request sets g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no signature, session or token validation
is_allowed looks up resource['grants'][user] using the spoofed string, so a file owner's name grants the 'delete' and 'write' actions
rename_file uses the same g.user in is_allowed(..., 'write')
The file is deleted from STORE after the check passes

finding.guards_checked: ensure_allowed and is_allowed check grants correctly for the user string they receive (acl.py:5-10). A missing header gives None, which is denied unless grants has a None key. No authentication middleware, signature check or proxy-header stripping exists in the code. I did not find any other file to check. Other observations: STORE[fid] raises KeyError (a 500 error, not a 403 or 404) for unknown ids, which is only a minor information and robustness issue. No object-creation endpoint exists, so grants cannot be attacker-set here.

verdict.guard_found: ACL check only (acl.py:5-10): is_allowed returns a bool, ensure_allowed aborts 403, and both results are used correctly at views.py:17 and :25. They check grants for the user string they receive. No authentication, signature check or header stripping in code. A trusted proxy outside this code may exist.
verdict.reason: Trace is accurate (views.py:11 trusts the raw X-Session-User-Verified header, acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, views.py:18 and :27 are the sinks), but whether this is exploitable depends on a front proxy that strips and sets the header, which the code can't show, and STORE (views.py:6) is never populated here, so the files and grants that would be attacked come from outside this code.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Upstream trusted identity middleware (per maintainer facts) supplies the X-Session-User-Verified header; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) and is_allowed (views.py:25, returns 403) gate the delete and rename.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace lines are accurate (views.py:11, 17-18, 25-27, acl.py:5), but views.py:11 reads an identity the maintainer states is populated by trusted upstream middleware, so a client-forged header is outside the stated threat model, and the ACL checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 correctly deny users without grants.
